en: The Fourth Act. [Dimensions: 24.3 cm x 16.5 cm x 1.9 cm x 2.4 cm] Now follows the section consisting of the connection with the hope of attaining the *patākā*.
The *garbhasandhi* (the "embryo" juncture) is indicated in the fourth and fifth acts. Regarding that, [it is said]: "The conduct of one whose purpose is the fruit..."
"It is an auxiliary to the primary [action]; and because of its connection with that, it is proclaimed as 'fruitful' (phalavat), like a banner.
(1) "Because of its connection with that" means because of its connection with the primary action; "fruitful" means possessing its own fruit.
And that fruit is the sovereignty of Tārā and so forth; and here, it is the conduct of Sugrīva that persists until the conclusion of the play.
[This is characterized by] hope for attainment through both the apprehension of means and the apprehension of obstacles.
"the possibility of attainment";
(2) *sambhava* means *sambhāvanā* (possibility); and (3) that [possibility] here refers to such [thoughts] as, "How can that [state] arise? and so forth.
"O Creator, when you are pleased," and so forth; "I wish to reach the end of enmity," and so forth.
By the recurrence of these two [verses], [the characteristics of] *abhūtāharaṇa* (false attribution) and the others [are established].
The mutual connection among the twelve elements is the *garbha-sandhi*. As it is said:
"The *garbha*, however, is the repeated searching for the seed that was seen and then lost. (7)
When the seed— that is, enthusiasm for the goal— is as if seen and then lost, its search through the investigation of means and obstacles is for the sake of attaining the fruit.

This is *niścaya* (certainty). And it consists of such passages as: "How [could] the descendant of Kṣatriyas [be capable] even in the subduing of Vālin? (8); "Daśaratha was desirous of a son" (9); and "By whom the entire family of kings was uprooted" (10). Its constituent parts are: *abhūtāharaṇa* (the fabrication of the non-existent), *mārga* (the path), *rūpa* (form), *udāharaṇa* (illustration), and *krama* (sequence).
"Collection (saṅgraha), inference (anumāna), as well as toṭaka, adhibala, agitation (udvega), confusion (sambhrama), and interruption (ākṣepa)—
these are the twelve limbs in their proper sequence. (11) Thus it is said.
Yawning,
due to the absence of sleep caused by anxiety arising from hearing the news of Mithilā reported by Śauṣkala; *vibhātā* = having shone forth in a distinguished manner.
She whose appearance [is such]—
the meaning is that dawn has occurred.
He states that very thing in sequence, beginning with "slightly awakened," and so forth.
*tandrāluḥ* means *tandrāśīlaḥ*, one who possesses laziness; [the suffix] *-āluc* is applied according to the rule beginning with *spṛhigṛhi* (Pāṇini 3.2.158). *Tāyante* means they become expanded.

The meaning is that even a substance situated at a distance is seen; this is a construction used in the reflexive sense (karmakartari), where the vowel lengthening occurs according to the rule *tanoter yaki*. Thus, they are "styāyantaḥ" (they coagulate).
In the reading—“they become joined,” meaning they become distinct; the root is *styai* or *ṣṭyai*, meaning “to sound” or “to collect.
Furthermore, there is a censure of the householder’s life because of their re-union. “Even now,” and so forth.
The meaning is that the crows, crying out at one moment and remaining silent at another,
being terrified and trembling with fear of the owls, ascertain the sounds of those [owls] through a correspondence of what they hear, for the purpose of summoning them to heaven. //1//

"Prācīm" and so forth. *Vāsakasajjikā* is one who has adorned her body for the arrival of her beloved; as it is said: "With joy, the *vāsakasajjā* adorns herself, thinking 'my beloved will come. (16) Here, "adornment" (*pariṣkāra*) refers to the purity of the early morning, and "decoration" (*maṇḍana*) refers to [the application of] cosmetics.
For the purpose of attracting him who has many beloveds; he says that very thing: "the beloved of the directions.
Regarding "Āgneyī" and so forth: [these are] the channels (sirās) that carry fire; the suffix *ḍhak* is applied in the sense of "belonging to this" (*tasyedam*) according to the rule:
"The suffix *ḍhak* should be stated after the words *agni* and *kali* in all cases. (*Pāṇini 4.3.71–72*).
By the rule "nāḍīmuṣṭyośca" (Pāṇini 3.2.30), the suffix *khaś* is applied; and by the principle "in a rule prescribing an upapada,
the mention of words such as *bhaya* and *āḍhya* implies the application of the rule of tadanta-vidhi," the word *āgneyanāḍī* functions as the upapada here because of the term *ādi* [in that rule].

By the rule "nāḍīmuṣṭyośca" (Pāṇini 5.1.55), the suffix *khaś* is applied after the word *dhmā* when preceded by *āgneyanāḍī*. [The term] *kṣaṇadā* [is used] because it brings great comfort during the night; and [the moon is called] *bhānu* because it is the friend (*bāndhava*) of the *koka* birds.
In that regard,
there is enjoyment, because it is the antidote to water lilies, and therein is sleep.

The meaning is that they cast [it down]; the sense is that they became joyful and their eyes blossomed like buds. When the king was thus occupied with his women, the ministers took charge of what ought to be done by him. //2//
He speaks specifically of the enjoyment of what is in front, beginning with the words "from here" (*itaḥ*) and so forth.
"Eastern" (*paurastyā*) means "situated in front" (*puro bhavā*); [this is derived] by the rule:
*dakṣiṇāpaścātpurasastyak*. (22)
"He reveals his rays upon the mountain peaks,
piercing the vital points in succession"; by this [it is meant] the locations of the digits (kalās), beginning with the thumb, of women.
The suppression [of her fear] is manifested through various such gestures:

having sealed her chest with the musk-paste ornamentation of her own breasts out of distrust toward the "teacher of new love" (navaratiguruh)— that is, the instructor of fresh amorous sports— she [acts].
*Projjhati* means she abandons. By this, her boldness (*prauḍhi*) is expressed. Or rather:
on the chest of her new teacher of love—the beloved—where her own musk-ornament has been transferred through a firm embrace, [she says], "O friends, do not..."
Thinking, "They might see [me]," she wipes away—that is, she cleanses—out of shame;
the verbal root *uñcha* is used in the sense of "removing" (according to Dhātupāṭha 23). By this, the middle [region] is described.

Because the equality of shame and passion is perceived through both the wiping away of tears with the leaf-like lips and the firm embrace, it is said: "The *madhyā* (intermediate heroine) is one whose youth is clearly manifest."
She who possesses equal degrees of modesty and passion should be known as one capable of sexual union ending in delusion. (24) Thus [ends the third section].
"This," and so forth. One whose purpose is jesting is a *vaihāsika*, that is, a *vidūṣaka* (jester); [the suffix] *ṭhak* is applied after words such as *kathā*;
thus, "a *vaihāsika* is one who makes *kilakilā* sounds."
And Vidūṣaka laughed: "Thus says Bhoja. *Vitapate* means "it rises";
the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used according to the rule *udvibhyāṃ tapaḥ*. [The meaning is: "The lord of lights (the sun) gently caused the lotus plants to blossom. By this—

The propitiation of a bold lover by an innocent woman who has felt a slight, fruitless resentment is suggested here; as it has been said: "He is called *dhṛṣṭa* (bold) whose offense is manifest and who is devoid of fear."
Thus it is said:
(27) "The innocent girl, possessing slight youth, is bewildered; her passion is overcome by bashfulness; her pride is fruitless and slight" (28). And: "Immediately... (29).

When the state of dependence has passed, the distinctive patterns of saffron paste, appearing inverted due to being transferred from a firm embrace upon the lover's chest, cause horripilation because they serve as reminders of their sexual union.
This one, too, is bold.
"From the abode of Priya," and so forth. *Karambitam* means "joined" (*lagnam*).
Keśava states: "'Lagna', 'karambita', 'śliṣṭa', 'sampṛkta', 'sevita', and 'sama' [are synonyms]. In the reading *karambhitāni*, it means "intermingled" (*sampṛktāni*).
"Karambha refers to curd-mixed barley meal," according to Amara. [The term] "acting like karambha" indicates contact with that [meal].
There is sparseness due to the absence of horripilation at the sites of nail-marks; one infers that this refers to some particular aspect of sexual enjoyment.

Because the horripilation [of the body] would otherwise be inexplicable. They speak—that is, they say—using the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) according to the rule "in the case of uttering distinct speech" (Pāṇini 1.3.48). These women, moreover, are bold.
This is the ornament known as "perceived by direct observation" (*pratyakṣadṛṣṭa*), because it describes the specific characteristics of the place, the departure of the woman, and her caste;
as it has been said: "according to the location, according to the time, and according to the form."
It is described as follows: "Whatever is perceived, whether directly or indirectly, that is 'seen' (dṛṣṭa);
it is considered to be like what has been seen. (32) //5//
"At dawn," and so forth. *Anurahasam* means in private (*ekānte*); *vṛttam* means activity (*vyāpāram*), specifically that which pertains to love (*mānmatham*).
The suffix *-ac* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.4.81: *anvavataptād rahasaḥ*. It does not bring happiness; the word "without speaking" (*anuktyā*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Shame arises from being newly married; "camatkāra" means trembling, born from the casting of the dice-stick.
Although not explicitly stated by the heroine, the nail-mark is a sign of sexual enjoyment.
"Kathayati" means "indicates"; the sense is that it makes known, "This is the place of the nail-mark.
Or alternatively, the hidden nail-mark is the agent [of the indication].
It reveals what occurred in secret.
By the word *camatkāra*, wonder (*āścarya*) is indicated, since trembling can also arise from astonishment. It is a marvel that even an insentient thing speaks.

From "starting from here" up to "he becomes one who is to be favored by the maṇḍala," this is the limb called the Path (*mārga*), because its nature consists in the proclamation of the principles (*tattva*).
As it has been said: "The Path is the proclamation of the principles. (35)
Thus [ends section] 6.

"Mu hūrtam" and so forth. By the use of the present participle suffix *śānac* in the word "kathyamānam," the repetition [of the speech] due to wonder is indicated. "Mānuṣyakam" means human effort, or the collection of humans;
the meaning is that it is an excellence beyond that, a state superior to the world.

By the rule *gottrokṣoṣṭraḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.136), the suffix *vuñ* is applied; by the rule *āpatyasya ca taddhite'nāti* (Pāṇini 6.4.151), there is the elision (*yalopa*) of the *ya* [of *yuvan*]; and by the rule *prakṛtyāke rājanyamanuṣyayuvānaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.163), because of the status of the base form (*prakṛtibhāva*), [the elision] does not take place.
"It is difficult" means that he is capable even of conquering Rāvaṇa; this is the sense.
He describes that very state with the words "that such [a thing]," and so forth.
"That such" means capable of breaking the bow of Śiva and other such feats; for this very reason, it is marvelous.
"In the world of humans" (manuṣyaloke): by this, it is stated that this place is unfit for the arising of divine splendor (*divya-tejas*). How does it arise without intention (*nirabhisandhi*)?
First of all, [the phrase] "it arises" [is not applicable].

"It is without underlying intention"; the sense is that it possesses intention indeed. "For now" means that there is a delay for the purpose of explaining the specific nature of that intention later on. That very [intention]—
He states the distinction: "those very [objects]," and so forth.
"Those very" means precisely such [objects], namely, those alone which are capable of being dispelled by such light; the sense is that this is because they are non-dharmic (adharmatvāt).
By means of this reason, which consists of reflection upon both these objects—
In our eyes,
regarding the object, the night shines forth— shines intensely— as if it were a day abundant with light.
The meaning is that it obstructs sleep. "Fie!"—the ellipsis is "upon us who experience such suffering. //7//
He says that very thing: "Having heard," and so forth.
Its quality of being difficult to hear arises from its resulting in one's own misfortune. By means of the cause that consists in the concealment of reflection, [he conceals it].

*sāvahitthavadanaḥ* means "with a face concealing its true expression," that is to say, for the purpose of denial; since there is no relationship of material cause and effect (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*) here, the compound is not a *caturthī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative compound) expressing purpose.
"Avahitthā is the concealment of one's internal state," according to Amara.

For this very reason, his smile was scattered toward Mithilā and other directions; it was a smile [expressing] that "this is of no consequence. Regarding the passage beginning with *helā*: *vāsaḥ* means *vāsanā* (latent impression). *Nāvati* means "does not gladden. Even though Rāma has conquered his senses...
"Terrified" means "I am distressed";
even those who are inferior to Indra and the other gods can be drawn [to one], but not—
The meaning is that Sītā has come into Rāma’s embrace;
this is a juncture-element (*sandhyantara*) named *saṃvṛti* (concealment).
As it has been said: "Concealment (*saṃvṛti*) is the self-concealing of one's own action. (41) //8//
"Dāruṇa" means because it has the sense of experiencing extreme suffering.
He says that very thing in the verse beginning with "When the Creator was pleased," etc. "Ahaṃyuḥ" means one possessed of egoism (*ahaṅkāra*).
Regarding the rule *ahaṃśubhamoryus* (Pāṇini 3.2.126):
that you have chosen fearlessness from others—namely, from the gods and so forth—is a wound to the heart;
for today Rāma has been born.
The sense is that calamity has come from this very human being. "Śāntam" means "may it be pacified"; the ellipsis is "the undesirable [consequences] rooted in our evil intentions."
The suffix *niṣṭhā* is used here according to the rule *āśaṃsāyāṃ bhūtavacca* (Pāṇini 3.3.132).

The phrase "you are the Ten-necked One" (*daśakandharo'si*) is a self-encouragement, signifying that he possesses ten times the strength of even a human being; it refers to one whose prowess is world-renowned.
Or thus. //9//
"Ah! [This expresses] his ignorance of what ought not to be done—the abandonment by Rāvaṇa, who is superior in prowess.
He says that very thing in the verse beginning with "Viśvāmitra," etc. We, however, are of maternal lineage.
Because they are *rākṣasas*, they are not fit for association; "not seen" means not investigated. "By the moonlight," "juṣṭāḥ" means frequented or served.
The meaning is that it refers to the time of prostration. //10//
Chāyā: Oh!

Beholding the lotus-faces of the princes of Raghu’s lineage, which spread a mass of splendor through the beauty of their gentle and lovely wedding attire—even while in this loathsome state of being a illusory human—[I am filled with wonder].
I have accomplished my purpose.
*Prāgbhāraḥ* means a multitude. Regarding the word *jugupsitena*: everyone [despises] their own kind.
The sense is that she held him in high esteem; by not accepting her human nature, she considered herself fulfilled, thinking that a vision [of him] would otherwise be difficult to obtain.
This is the subsidiary limb (aṅga) called *māyā* within the *sandhi*; as it has been said: "Māyā is the fabrication of deception" (45).
Chāyā: Oh, such is she!
The nature of virtues is such that they bring happiness even when fallen into the hands of their opposites;
that is what is meant by "of such a kind. It means that the virtues of even an enemy are of such a nature.
The meaning is that they cause joy.
Chāyā: How is it that my maternal grandfather is right here on the upper terrace of the watchtower?
*Aṭṭālaka* refers to a structure atop a wall; it is a shelter situated on its summit.
*Pragrīva* would refer to a shelter located on a *mattālamba*.
"Mattavāraṇa" means "an elephant in rut," according to Keśava.

Chāyā: Alas, how ill-fitted is the lot of those who perform evil deeds, since now, with eyes moistened by sleeplessness and the cavity of his mouth stretched wide by yawning at every moment, he beholds the burden of his harsh task situated within his own heart.
Someone or other appears as if [present];
due to the absence of sleep caused by anxiety over impending misfortune, there is yawning. "Seen" means inferred.
The cleverness of the expression is that the internal object is seen through the opening of the mouth;
that is to say, another form has arisen due to suffering. [The commentary] says: "Or rather, even of the universal..."
The office of minister is indeed a weighty one,
especially for our lord Rāvaṇa, whose conduct is fierce and solely intent on the passion for daring exploits; I know me alone [to be fit for it].
"He remains waiting," [meaning] "until I approach him.
"Of a common person"; that is to say, even of a mere king. "Specifically" refers to this [person].

The sense is that because of the excess of ill-discipline, there is a multiplicity of remedies; regarding this, Kāmandaka says: "Of a king who is arrogant with pride, like an elephant in rut that is difficult to restrain..."
"Indeed, leaders who associate with one of unjust conduct incur reproach.
(47) Shadow: Noble sir, I salute you.
Chāyā: Noble sir, when Daśaratha had arrived and the auspicious *godāna* ceremony for the princes had been completed, I entered the city of Mithilā.
The "gift of a cow" (*godāna*) is a specific sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*) preceding marriage.
(48) It is said to be "highly manifest" because, in the absence of marriage, it is impossible for a younger brother to marry while an elder brother remains unmarried.
Chāyā: "Indeed so!
It is a 'bad play' (durnāṭaka). The sense is that he himself, like a stage director (sūtradhāra), is the impeller of all.
He says that very thing in the verse beginning with "yajñopaplava" and so forth.
"Pariṇataḥ" means aged;
one whose age is such that he is no longer fit for separation from his son.

The sense is that "being skilled in battle" refers to requesting a king who is merely a possibility after abandoning a king who has already been secured; furthermore, depending upon another for one's own objective— which consists of the destruction of the demon— is hypocrisy (*kuhanā*).
*Vidhau* means in the scripture (*śāstre*); *vinīya* means having trained (*śikṣitvā*). By this, its status as a rule (*kalpyatva*) is stated. *Te* refers to Subāhu and the others;
*jaghnire* means they were slain (*ghātitāḥ*). The causative sense (*ṇyartha*) is inherent, and the verb is in the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) in the passive voice (*karmani*).
*Itaḥ* means from here, that is, beyond this point. *Kuhanā* is false conduct (*mithyācaryā*) due to greed and other motives. "Kuhanā... [is the definition].

"From greed comes the fabrication of a false deportment" (Amara, 49); *īryāpatha* refers to meditation and so forth, meaning "deceit. By that [deceit], he is like a *viṭa*—that is, a deceiver—or else his hypocrisy (*kuhanā*) is under his control. *Vaṭu* means "fickle. Regarding the form *kāriṣyate*, the augment *iṭ* is applied as if it were *ciṇ* by the rule "syasicsīyuṭ... (Pāṇini 6.4.62).
Because the augment *iṭ* (ciṇvadiṭ) is treated as if it were non-existent (*asiddhavat*) by the rule "asiddhavadatrābhāt," there is the elision of the suffix *ṇi* by the rule "ṇeraniṭi. //11//
Chāyā: Noble sir, it is indeed so. However, I have seen that Brahmin even surpassing the great seer Vasiṣṭha;
the sense is that he is superior even to Vasiṣṭha.

*Sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original) means performing the function that was to be performed by the original element. *Kṣatra-kārya* refers to activities such as violence and so forth. *Brahman* is the Veda; that which pertains to it is *brāhma*, namely the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*).
That which pertains to a *brāhmaṇa* is *brāhmaṇya*, namely the cultivation of austerity. All sages are indeed twice-born (*dvija*).
"But this one is Trija"—this is a joke.
"Adhīyan" means studying without difficulty; [it is formed] by the rule *iṅ-dhāryoḥ śatrakṛcchriṇi* (Pāṇini 3.2.130).

The suffix is *śatṛ*. *Avarīṇam* means "insignificant" (*tuccham*); it is derived from the root *rī* preceded by the prefix *ava-* in the sense of "going" or "seeking" (Dhātupāṭha 54), with the *niṣṭhā* suffix; the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* in the *niṣṭhā* suffix occurs according to the rule "after [roots] beginning with *lū*" (Pāṇini 8.2.44).
"Avarīṇa" means "reproached," according to Amara. The sense is that qualities arise from association (*saṃsargaja*). [The verb] "pariṇaṃsyate" means...

In the case of the agent being the object (*karmakartṛ*), the *ātmanepada* [suffix] is used. He states this very point with the words beginning "lack of discipline" (*avinaya*). The reading is "from a rogue" (*phaṇāt*).
Even the practice of learning, though it brings about good character (*sauśīlya*), [may come] from a rogue.

If [the light] comes from the teacher, it brings about only agitation; for even though the light of a jewel destroys the darkness that brings fear of snakes, if it comes from the hood of a venomous serpent—this is the ellipsis—it certainly intensifies that fear. This is according to the rule beginning with *bhṛśādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.12).
The suffix *kyaṅ* is also used in the sense of *cvī*. //12//
"To seize"—the word "Sītā" is to be supplied as the object. "Uttiṣṭhamānaḥ" means "exerting oneself"; the middle voice (ātmanepada) is used according to the rule *udo'nūrdhvakarmaṇi* (Pāṇini 1.3.24).
"Pratikartavyaḥ" means "to be warded off."
The meaning is: "By what means shall we fulfill his longing?
Shadow: "Noble sir, surely not by avoiding force."
Some other means is being considered! The implication is that there is no other alternative.

*Vīraprakāṇḍam* means "a praiseworthy hero"; the compound is formed according to [Pāṇini 2.1.66] *praśaṃsāvacanaiśca*; [Amarakośa 3.3.194cd–195ab] states: "*prakāṇḍa*, *udgha*, and *tallaja*—these are words expressing excellence."
Thus says Amara. Regarding the phrase "mahādoṣa" and so forth:
*mahādoṣaḥ* means that which has great undesirable results (*anarthaphala*). By such [a person]; that is to say, by one who had broken the bow of Hara.
Through these three adjectives, the excellence of strength, destiny, and human effort is indicated.
These have been stated.

He says that very thing in the verse beginning with "dostambha" (stiffness of the arms), and so forth. "The ostentation of pride" (*darpa-ḍambara*) means its manifestation. "It does not quiver" (*na vispandate*) means it does not move; the sense is that movement indicates pride. It does not... [text fragment ends]

He begins—meaning, he commences the stringing of the bow; because this act is synonymous with the demand "Sītā must be given to me," there is shame. Having reflected—that is, having deliberated—Rāma smiled.
Because of the pursuit of skill in intellect; salutation [is performed] when taking up weapons, as prescribed by the heroic convention (*vīrasamaya*);
*āñcita* means drawn back; "of such a kind" means thus.
Description of the Greatness of the Bow. //13//
"How so? and so forth. "In that"—meaning, in such an experience. By the term "lord of the night-stalkers," he expresses his being the sole refuge of the family and his victory over unrighteousness.
"An assailant" means one who abducts a wife; as it has been said: "One who sets fire [to a house], one who administers poison..."
"One with a weapon in hand, a robber of wealth, and likewise those who seize land or wives—these six are *ātatāyin*s (assassins). [The opponent says: "We grant this. [The author replies:
"How can we accept this basis which results in harm to our own master? This is the meaning.
Chāyā: As determined by the maternal grandfather. "Determined" means presented; the word "matter" (*kāryam*) is to be supplied as the object.
Chāyā: Oh, the power of Time!
Such is the majesty that even regarding the great king Rāvaṇa— who has playfully imprisoned the Fortune of Victory of the three worlds— it is deliberated in this manner.
The word "evam" (thus) refers to the lack of capability. It is a marvel that even for one who has conquered the three worlds, the victory over Rāma is difficult to achieve.
The phrase "kiñca" (moreover) indicates that it is not merely a matter of innate capability.
The meaning is that there is also [the merit] arising from being accepted by Brahmins and deities.
He states this very point with the words "even the sage," and so forth. "The sage" refers to Kauśika. By this, the purity of the tradition is expressed. It is a great festival for the deities.

"Because of the knowledge of Rāma's majesty: 'He is just that much'—by means of an illustration, it has been stated that He is indefinable both in terms of His means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) and His essential nature (*svarūpa*).
[The term *guṇakrītīm* means] purchased or won over by qualities, that is, by the instruments [of perception]; from the root *krī* (to buy)."

The suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to the rule *karaṇapūrvāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.79). The meaning is that since Indra and the others are to be commanded, the three worlds as well are to be commanded. This being the case, if there is a contradiction with this [scripture], then...
Under the pretext of authority, wickedness *vipariṇamate*—that is, it bears fruit;
the sense is that people would designate them as "wicked" on account of the guise of authority. (*Padaṃ* occurs in the senses of "word" and "authority").

Regarding "vyavahārāpadeśayoḥ" (in the sense of legal procedure and pretext), the *Viśvaprakāśa* states [this]. Alternatively: *padam* means "authority" (*adhikāra*), and *vipariṇamate* means "it undergoes a transformation" (*vyatyayam āpadyate*); that is, having cast aside sovereignty, it assumes the authority of wickedness.
The sense is that [it] would fall. //14//
Chāyā: What doubt is there? At that great festival of marriage, everything was witnessed by me directly.
"Everything" refers to Rāma’s strength, enthusiasm, and so forth. [The phrase] "the killing with a single clod of earth" means:
The meaning is that just as for those disputing over even a single clod of earth, death itself ultimately results,
so too would that same logic apply to us who desire merely a maiden.

Regarding "nārācaiḥ" and so forth: "priyambhāvukaiḥ" means "by those who are dear"; [it is derived] from the root *bhū* with the suffix *uka*, denoting the agent (*kartari*).

The suffix *khukañ* is applied [after the word] *bhuvaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.85), and that [suffix signifies] "one who increases that" (*tadvardhakatvāt*). For him, water is indeed blood (*kṣataja*); the substitution of *uda-* for *udaka-* occurs by the rule "in a name, *udaka* becomes *uda*" (Pāṇini 6.1.129). *Atha* means "immediately thereafter."
*Nyupta* means given to the ancestors; Amara states: "The gift to the ancestors is called *nivāpa*. [The hero], being a descendant of Bhṛgu (*bhārgava*), having slain Kārtavīrya and others...
The story is that he offered handfuls of sesame seeds (*tilāñjali*) to the ancestors in those lakes of blood.

"Of him who devours the *bāhujāḥ* (those born from the arms)—the Kṣatriyas": this refers to the rule of eating after the ritual libation (*tarpaṇa*). "Of one who is being expelled"—that is, of one whose liberation (*nirvāṇa*) is imminent.
"Crushing" means breaking;
"fuel" refers to wood intended for burning and kindling. The meaning is that even though I am dispassionate, anger arose upon hearing of the breaking of my preceptor’s bow. //30//
"Child," and so forth; the sense is "by means of ignorance" and "without effort.
"Of such a kind" means having the nature of being fragile. "Incidental" means accomplished without primary effort, by the very effort of attraction.
By the statement "it is broken," negligence and its influence are expressed; by "it was not reckoned by me," ignorance and pride are likewise expressed. //31//
"Mahāsena," and so forth: he was liberated even while alive; the meaning is that out of extreme compassion, the arrows released him without his life-force having departed.
Or rather, "living" is said precisely because he is liberated; just as one released from the fangs of Yama lives, so too does he live even with the arrow extracted. "Twice" means two times.
Regarding arrows, which are a specific kind of grass: Kumāra was born in a thicket of *śara* grass.

"From the arrows"—that is, from the presence of the shafts. Regarding the repetition of the action, there is the irregularity [of using *suc*] according to the rule "after *dvi*, *tri*, and *catur*, *suc* [is added].
This is because the forest-fortress is difficult to enter. The use of the third person (*ayam*) is an indirect speech (*parokṣokti*) arising from the force of his own anger. //32//

"Without having reflected," and so forth. That there was no counting [of faults] out of pride, but rather due to a lack of discernment, is *vinaya* (humility/modesty). As for the fact that they were not even objects of pride, let alone objects of reflection, this constitutes *nindā* (censure).
"Among women," and so forth: among women, your mother alone is the mother of a pre-eminent hero, and no other;
for Gaurī was ashamed because of her son's defeat.
The praise is: "I wonder why I was not born in the form of Reṇukā? The censure, however, is: "Your mother is the mother of a hero among women alone, but not of a hero among men."

Since this wonder regarding your prowess arose for Pārvatī alone and not for the Supreme Lord—on the grounds that "women do not possess specialized knowledge"—the address "O hero among women" (*strīṣu pravīra*) may be intended as a sarcastic remark. In that case, the phrase "your mother herself is a mother who seeks the death of her own son" is a mocking expression. [The name] Viśākha.

His arms and feet, though possessing branches [limbs], are as if non-existent because they are incapable of performing their functions; this is a censure implying, "What excellence is there in the victory over the lowly?
Regarding the term *spṛha*, it takes the dative case according to the rule *spṛher īpsitaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.36).

This is the ornament called *garhaṇā* (reproach), because it takes the form of exposing faults under the guise of praising virtues; as it has been said: "Where one praises virtues by way of mentioning faults..."
Or, while proclaiming virtues, one should point out faults, for that is indeed censure. (144) //33//
"Anubhava," and so forth. By repeated consideration, [it becomes] worn out (*yātayāmā*).

"Naḥ" means "of us" (*asmākam*), [referring to] our practice of hymns (*stotracaryām*). However, in the case of censure (*nindā*), there is a compound with the word *na*; [this refers to] the word *na*. (145) [This is] the word *na*.
"Virodha" means contradiction; "nastotra" means refutation, and its practice [is what is meant]; the sense is that verbal harshness is not the duty of a Kṣatriya.
From Kauśika: "upajñā" refers to that whose first knowledge is such;
for it is said, "upajñā would be the first knowledge. (146)
Thus says Amara; that is to say, as taught by Kauśika. *Goṣṭhī* means a social gathering;
its *vinoda* (diversion) is battle.

*Udyacchamānaḥ* means *sannahyamānaḥ* (equipping oneself); [the suffix] *śānac* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.147 (*samudāṅbhyaḥ* etc.). *Kālaṃ na kṣipati* means he does not let time pass; he does not delay.
That is to say, it endures. //34//
"Even Viśvāmitra"— the implication is that it is not only me alone. "Let it be so for now"— this means that the overt insult will come later.
The intention is: "But now, let him be somewhat formidable.

Regarding the phrase "bhūmātram" and so forth: *bhūmātram* means "the earth alone"; as Amara states, "*mātram* [is used] in the sense of totality (*kārtsnye*) or restriction (*avadhāraṇe*). This [earth] is "how much?"—that is, very little.
The meaning is that because of the limited nature of his prowess, it was not sufficient.
Regarding the term *triḥsaptakṛtvaḥ*: *triḥ* means three repetitions of the action, according to the rule *dvitricaturbhyaḥ suc*; *sapta* means seven.

The repetitions of the action—seven times; [according to] Pāṇini 5.4.17, "the suffix *kṛtvasuc* is used after a numeral in the sense of counting the repetition of an action"; thereafter, [the rule for] the qualifier...
The compound is formed according to the rule *viśeṣyeṇa bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.57). *Triḥsaptakṛtvaḥ* means twenty-one times.
*Bhavādṛśena* means by one such as you, that is, by one who is incomparable.

"It is being carried away by you"; this is the present tense (laṭ) in the passive voice of the causative (ṇic). The meaning is that even though the earth was conquered by you, because you repeatedly neglected it for the sake of the sport of battle, it was carried away by the enemies. "Ḍimbha" means a child.
"Navabāhu" means one with tender arms.
"Vīravratam" means battle. "Īdṛśam" means such a terrible [battle]; he shall conquer it twenty-one times.
He is worthy of honor by birth alone; how much more so by his prowess—this is praise. [Alternatively, it may be] censure.
"But—by someone like you"—meaning, there is no one inferior to you;
for by you only the earth itself has been conquered, and not another world; even that was but a small portion, because it is limited; and even that was impossible to carry out.

"It is being carried off by enemies! Though I am but a child, my arms are not yet withered. This refers to the breaking of the bow, reflecting on how terrible such a thing is. For Brahmins are to be honored by Kshatriyas because of their seniority, but not because of prowess.

Regarding the word *krodhāt*: its status as an ablative (*apādāna*) is established by the rule *jugupsā-virāma-*, etc. (Pāṇini 1.4.24). The intended meaning is that this anger of yours will result in misfortune in the future.
This is an example [of the figure of speech] because its meaning is hidden yet identical [to the literal one].
This is indeed an ornament; as it has been said: "A sentence whose meaning is hidden yet equivalent [to another] is considered an *udāharaṇa* (illustration). (155) //35//

"Aho!"—this expresses wonder because even a child’s manner of speech resembles that of a great hero. Regarding the passage beginning with "vinaya" (modesty): [he is] "niculita," meaning covered or concealed, by modesty which contains within it a lack of modesty.
Amarasimha states: "nicolaḥ" means a covering cloth (*pracchadapaṭaḥ*). It refers merely to a concealment.

It is observed as *akrama*, meaning "decrease" (*apakarṣa*); if the reading is *aṅkana*, it means "blemish" (*kalaṅka*). A *krakaca* is a specific type of iron tool for splitting wood and the like. The plural form in *vacobhiḥ* [is used].

This is with the intention that "even a single instance of insult can be endured, but not many"; as it has been said: "A forgiving person may perhaps tolerate [an offense] slightly or by way of non-repetition at will, but [he cannot endure it] when it occurs through intensive repetition (kriyāsamabhihāreṇa)."
"Who could forgive one who acts with hostility? (157). The implication is that while I am armed, your being unarmed is contrary to the code of warriors (*vīrasamaya*). //36//
"Aloud" (*uccaiḥ*): this is spoken aloud in accordance with the intensity of his anger.
"In the matter of protecting the three worlds," etc.: *śauṇḍaḥ* means intoxicated or unrestrained. *Unmaryādaḥ* means one who has transgressed all bounds.
"Atitrātā" means "intoxicated";
according to Amara, "matte, śauṇḍa, utkaṭa, kṣība" [are synonyms for intoxicated].
The dissolution of the color produced from the arms into the arms themselves is an instance of the effect being identical to its cause (*kāryasya kāraṇe laya*).

The sense is that [the fire] is extinguished by this means. Due to their common nature (*sājātyāt*), one's own arms are also the cause [of its extinction]. The blazing [of the fire] arises from anger; for the defeat of a father must not be tolerated by a son.
The statement regarding [his] being a son. //37//
"Non-occurrence," and so forth. "Occurrence" (*pravṛtti*) refers to the operation (*vyāpāra*) characterized by denotation (*abhidhā*).
Its "object" (*viṣaya*), meaning its cause (*nimitta*), is the universal (*jāti*) which constitutes the denotable content. [The word] is "devoid of that.
"Extending" (*vitanvataḥ*) means "performing"; here the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) is used in the sense of the cause (*hetu*). (159)

The meaning is "for the sake of performing. Because he destroyed every individual instance of the warrior caste (*kṣatra-jāti*), it is a figurative expression to say that he destroyed the warrior caste itself. This refers to the nature of the slaughter of all warriors.

Since you have made the earth the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the sacrifice, you have no further duty to perform; therefore, your weapon is "dry," meaning fruitless—it must simply be cast away. //38//

"One must be Janaka"—this is the limb called inference (*anumāna*), because Janaka-hood is inferred from the voice as a mark (*liṅga*). As it has been said: "Inference is the conjecture [of a property] from a mark" (160).
"From the disciple of Sūrya": Yājñavalkya, out of resentment toward his own teacher, vomited up the Veda he had studied and remained in the ear of a horse.
The narrative should be understood as follows: Sūrya studied the Śukla Yajurveda, which has the alternative name Vājasaneyi. *Brahmasiddhānta* means Vedānta.
*Gṛhīta* means accepted (*aṅgīkṛta*). *Anurodha* means following (*anusaraṇa*).
He says that very thing with the words beginning "the earth" (*avanim*), etc. "Having assailed" (*abhyavaskandya*) means having conquered.
By the word *avabhṛtha*, the sacrifice is indicated. In that regard:

*Bhṛtakāḥ* refers to those who live on wages in the form of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), namely the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); as Amara states: "A *bhṛtaka* is one who eats for hire, a laborer, and he is also called *vaitanika*. How does he cease? He certainly would not cease. [This is used] in the sense of censure (*garhā*); according to the rule: "The optative (*liṅ*) is optionally used after *katham* when expressing censure. (Pāṇini 3.3.143).
The suffix *laṭ* [is used] in the sense of "and" (*ca*). The meaning is that for one who has conquered kings, abstaining from even a single [act] is censurable. //39//
Regarding the passage beginning with *bhṛgu*: *vaimatya* means anger; the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied because it belongs to the *dṛḍha*-class (Pāṇini 5.1.123).
That which possesses compassion is *karuṇa*; the suffix *ac* is applied because it belongs to the *arśas*-class (Pāṇini 5.2.127).

In the phrase *putrabhāṇḍe*, it means "in the capital wealth consisting of a son"; Amara states that "the word *bhāṇḍa* refers to the capital of a merchant. (166) Regarding the matter of giving, *sthūlalakṣaḥ* means "one who gives much. (167)
"Vadānya, sthūlalakṣa, dānaśauṇḍa, and bahuprada" are synonyms for a generous donor, according to Amara. [This applies] to you, who have conquered the three worlds.
The meaning is that a fool is not an object for anger;
this [act] is called *sāma* (conciliation) because it consists in following the will of one who is angry.
This is a sub-division (*antaraṅga*) of the *sandhi* [sentiment]; as it has been said: "In that context, *sāman* (conciliation) is a pleasing speech that reveals one's own compliance. //40//

"Because of this name": by the friendship born from the identity of the names of your son and mine; that is to say, because of the sameness of our names, you are as venerable to me as you are to him. Regarding this, Śrīharṣa says: "Either the sharing of a single name, or being raised together..."
"Dwelling in the same place, habitual seeing one another,
hearing of mutual affection, providing assistance in one's absence, or sharing similar character— these seven are the causes for loving-kindness. (169) Thus it is said.
He speaks specifically of the conduct of heroes, beginning with "O Puramathana" and so forth. *Ahardivam* means "always";
it is a *nipāta* (irregular formation) according to the rule beginning with *acatura*. *Arciḥ* refers to that which is called anger. *Gurutiraskartā* means one who insults his teacher.

The sense is that he must not be overlooked, but must indeed be slain; this is the "vow of heroes" (*vīrasamaya*). In the phrase *raghujanaka*, both the instigator and the one being instigated are referred to.
He states the state of being subject to punishment:
*uśanti* means they desire; the verbal root is *vaśa* in the sense of "desire" (*kāntau*);
*kāntiḥ* means desire. [This occurs] by water alone for fire.
"Peace" is an utterance of tears. //41//

*Atiprasaktaḥ* means *atikrāntaḥ*, i.e., one who has transgressed the bounds; the sense is that there is no fault in violating a rule when it concerns urgent matters (*ātipātika-kāryeṣu*). *Pāṃsanaḥ* means a defiler.
Regarding the phrase "this one," etc.: *ekaḥ* refers to Yājñavalkya; *yasya antare* means "in whose midst."

"You are established in austerity. "Varṣīyān" means "old"; the substitution of "varṣa" for the word "vṛddha" occurs according to the rule beginning with "priyasthira" (Pāṇini 6.4.157). "Titikṣyase" means "you are patient" or "you endure."

Regarding the sense of "forgiveness" (*kṣamā*), [the rule] *agūp-tij-kid-bhyaḥ san* (Pāṇini 3.1.5) applies. The intention is that [the word] *nāmagrāhī* is used here because the governing rule for *dhanur-grahaṇa* (taking up a bow) is far removed. *Samāpyase* means you are being harmed. *Amṛtam* is the remnant of the sacrifice (*yajña-śeṣa*); as it is said: "The *amṛta* is the *vighasa*."
"Yajñaśeṣa and bhojanaśeṣa [denote] the remnants of a sacrifice and the remnants of a meal," so says Amara. //42//
Of the "encounter," that is, of the battle;
"intensive repetition" means frequency.
They "fall into calamity," that is, they become bewildered; the meaning is that they fall into error. "Like another," that is, like a commoner. "Abandoned."

The sense is that the weapon must not be taken up again. Alternatively, "not other" (*apara*) means "prior" (*pūrva*); thus, even though it was [previously] understood from the words of Cyavana and others, now—

The meaning is that you have fallen into a state as if unawakened. It is called a "piśācī" because it is the cause of delusion, or because it is the cause of activities such as improper dancing and so forth;
[one who is] possessed by a piśācī...

This is indeed the action: the patron (*yājya*) is one who is to be caused to sacrifice, [namely] Janaka. "First I shall conciliate him"—the meaning of the word *tāvat* is that afterwards there shall be a rebuke.
"nṛpastas... and so forth. "Rasikaḥ" means one who possesses affection;
the sense is that because he is a performer [of his duties], even if he commits an offense, he is not to be harmed. By the word "bhuja," prowess is indicated.
It is observed; the meaning is that they possess innate valor.
"Something arrogant" means haughty even in the absence of any cause for pride, while I stand here. [The word] *vidhātā* [is in the] periphrastic future (*luṭ*). //43//
"O sinner!"—by these two successive vocatives, he expresses her lack of purity of lineage and her cruelty.
"Lifeless" means devoid of essence. "Whether such or otherwise" means even if she has committed an offense. "Transgressing"—the word "the boundary" is to be supplied as the object.

Regarding "from Brahmanic luster" (*brahmavarcasāt*): the suffix *ac* is applied by the rule *brahmahastibhyāṃ varcasaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.78). Its status as an ablative (*apādāna*) is established by the rule *bhītrārthānāṃ bhayahetuḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.25).
The intended meaning is "I shall curse."
The word *hāsaḥ* signifies contempt. *Brahmabandhu* means the lowest of Brahmins;
according to the *Viśvakośa*: "The term *brahmabandhu* is used for the censure or designation of twice-born men.
*Bandhakī* means an unchaste woman; [the word *bandhaki-apatya* refers to her offspring] because it belongs to the *śubhrādi* group.
[The suffix] *ḍhak* [is applied], and by virtue of [the word] belonging to the *kalyāṇī*-class, the suffix *inaṅ* is added.
For it is heard in scripture that Ahalyā was enjoyed by Indra. Precisely for this reason, [it is so].

*Pāṃsanaḥ* means a defiler of the family. He makes a formal declaration—preceded by a wager in the form of an axe and renunciation—regarding the cowardice of the Raghus and the lack of Brahminhood in the Sage, beginning with the words "They would do... and so forth. *Aṅkurāḥ*...
Rāma and the others— would they even speak of it, let alone put it into practice? Even if they were to mention it incidentally, then the hand of emperors, ever eager to draw the bowstring—
Indeed, he wields an axe as the instrument for cutting—fie on this wielding!
"The host of Brahmins" (*brahmagaṇaḥ*) means a multitude of Brāhmaṇas; it is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (a class based on general form), such as: "I am born of distinguished parents..."

If, by being devoid of such a restrictive rule as "one who is a Brāhmaṇa," there were instead a rule such as "one who wears a topknot and a sacred thread is a Brāhmaṇa," then they too would be so. Among them, you are intended to be a Brāhmaṇa.
If that were so, then surely the hand, eager to uproot the kusa grass, would have taken up the axe— the instrument for cutting the sacrificial fuel— instead.
"Fie on this wearing [of the marks]!
I shall lay down my axe in both cases"—this is the sense. "They are not heroes, and you are no Brahmin"—this is the sense. //44//

"Thou," and so forth. *Vedavān* means one who has studied the Vedas. *Sanābhi* means a kinsman; as Amarasimha states: "Those who are *sapiṇḍas* are *sanābhayas*. Since you are the son of Bhṛgu, the son of Brahmā, you are *Svāyambhuva*.

Because of the rule "A grammatical operation conditioned by a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is not obligatory" (Pāṇini 1.1.56), the designation *bha* being prior [to the application of the rule], there is no substitution of *guṇa* according to "The *guṇa* substitute for *o*" (Pāṇini 6.1.97); rather, there is only the substitution of *uvaṅ*.
Therefore, by virtue of its weight (*gurutva*), it is *masṛṇa* = smooth/glossy. Hence, not.

*Truṭati* means it is not cut; the sense is that it does not break. The meaning is that it becomes rough and easily severed, rather than being smooth and sticky. *Kudṛṣṭi* means false knowledge. One who belongs to the lineage of a teacher (*gurukulya*) is not...
The sense is that he is to be killed. //45//
Regarding "Daśaratha": it does not function, nor does it proceed;
this is stated because of the cutting nature of the axe. Regarding "purojanman" and so forth: this single word is a qualifier of the word *jana*.

The meaning of the second [member] is its connection with this place and this time, and that [meaning] is construed with the *parikara* (accessory); the sense is "bound without delay," or else there is repetition (*vīpsā*) in this very sense.
The sense is that he has transgressed the command of his guru, the Dharma, and public censure. *Dīkṣā* means resolve;
in that context, *parikara* refers to the bow and other equipment. //46//
"With contempt" means that because Lakṣmaṇa was a child, he was not an object of anger;
[this refers to] Rāma’s embarrassment.
[This is] due to hearing Lakṣmaṇa’s words of ill-behavior. "Because of his youth" means that a child commits no offense whatsoever in an improper act;
this refers to the smile of Bhārgava directed toward Rāma.
This indicates the impossibility of anger. *Amṛṣyamāṇam* means not enduring.
Regarding the phrase "following you" and so forth: because he is subordinate to you, [he follows] only through your victory.
The sense is: "He has been conquered.
"Varam" means somewhat superior; the sense is that even a mere heroic discourse still exists [in him].
He says that very thing with the words beginning with *prāk* and so on. *Kṣuraprāḥ* are a particular kind of arrow.

*Śiraḥ* means a peak and also the place of the frontal globes (*kumbha*). *Dantāvalaḥ* means an elephant; [the suffix] *valac* is applied here according to Pāṇini 5.2.113: *danta-śikhāt saṃjñāyām*. [The word refers to] the Mānasa lake.
It is well known that swans emerge from the caves of Krauñca Mountain,
and that pearls are found within the frontal globes of elephants.
As it has been said: "Pearls are said to originate from eight sources: those produced by clouds, elephants, fish, serpents, bamboos, conch shells, boars, and oysters. (189)
"Having scattered" means having dispersed. "Fully accomplished" means completed;
the sense is that it has been brought to perfection. For a lion indeed becomes a slayer of elephants.
"By way of" means by manner or by cause. "They [felt] curiosity."
*Ābhigāmika* means relating to the qualities that cause one to be approached (*ābhigāmikaguṇa*); the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *tasyedam* (Pāṇini 4.3.120).
*Abhigama* refers to being worthy of being served by the world; those qualities which merit this are the *ābhigāmika* qualities.
In the word *tadarhati* (191), the suffix *ṭhak* is applied;

because it belongs to the *anuśatikādi* group, there is vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) in both parts of the compound; and these [qualities] are lineage, character, and so forth. This has been stated by Kauṭilya:
Having enumerated family, conduct, and so forth— it is said: "These [qualities], along with learning, honesty, and generosity, constitute the eightfold group."

The means of accomplishment consists of victory over the two, five, and six [planets], the avoidance of the seven, skill in expedients (*upāya*), and righteousness (*dharma*); these and others are auspicious actions.
Those qualities which have for their purpose the arising of both seen and unseen results are called *guṇas*.
These are the approaches. (193) //47//
"Difficult to discern," and so forth. "This" refers to my curiosity. "The fruit" is the form of victory produced by that curiosity of mine.
"Pertaining to battle" means it is capable of leading to battle; [according to Pāṇini 5.1.107] "tasmai prabhavati. (194)
By [the rule] beginning with *ityādinā*, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied. This [word], *durvijñānam*, means "difficult to be known" (*duḥkhena vijñeyam*).
Regarding the sense of the suffix *khal* (as in *durvijñāna-kara*), the suffix *yuc* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.3.127] *āto yuc*.
The form *ā* is used in the sense of anger (*kope*). [The term] *kṣetrīkaroti* means "he makes into a field," that is, "he makes into a location."

This, consisting of a threat upon hearing of the [hero's] physical characteristics and ill-discipline, is the intermediate juncture (*saṃdhyantara*) element called "Punishment" (*daṇḍa*). As it has been said:
"Punishment, however, is the threatening of those who are undisciplined and the like, by means of both sight and hearing. (197)
*Yantritaḥ* means bound.
*Sūnṛtām* means that which is both true and pleasant; as Amarasimha states: "The word *sūnṛtam* refers to what is pleasant and true. (198)
From "Starting from here" up to "I fear rashness" (199), this section, which consists of the manifestation of mutual power, is the ornament named *śobhā* (beauty);
as it has been said: "Śobhā is the manifestation of power."
"It is said that [the suffix *ka*] is applied to young people in the sense of mutual relation" (200). Thus, *kavacaharaḥ*;
"he who takes (*harati*) armor (*kavacam*)"—that is, he who goes having put on armor—is so called;
this is by the rule "and in the sense of age" (201).
The suffix *ac* is applied to the root *harati*;
it means "one who seizes. [He seizes] by means of weapons alone, and not by pleasant words.
Regarding "rājanye" and so forth: "vaivasvatebhyaḥ" means "to the offspring of Vivasvat."
*Ācāryakam* means the state of being a teacher (*ācāryatvam*); the suffix *vuñ* is applied according to the rule beginning with "after a word ending in *ya* as an upadhā" (Pāṇini 5.1.132).
*Caryām* means conduct (*ācāram*). Thus, by virtue of enduring insults. *Gotrākṣepī* means one who defiles a family (*kuladūṣakaḥ*). *Kalaṅkaḥ* means censure (*nindā*).

“Vajralepa” (adamantine plaster) refers to a substance called *vajra* that is difficult to remove; the sense is that it is forbidden for a Kṣatriya who is endowed with noble birth and weapons to endure insults and the like. //48//

"Born," and so forth. "Learned in the Vedas" (*śrotriya*) indicates the perfection of his conduct. "Seen" means not merely one who has received instruction, but rather one who has directly perceived [the truth] and has mastered the divine weapons and the Vedas.
Bhāvaḥ. Sāhasikyam = the action of a reckless person (sāhasika); it means "acting with rashness."

The suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule "ojaḥ-saha-ambhasā vartate" (Pāṇini 4.4.27), and thereafter the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied according to the rule "guṇavacana... (Pāṇini 5.1.123). //49//

Durmukha means one who speaks much; according to Amarasimha, "durmukha, mukhara, and ābaddhamukha" [are synonyms]. Svastivācanika means [one who performs] the recitation of benedictions (svastivācana).
He lives; [the suffix] *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule *vetanādibhyo jīvati* (Pāṇini 4.4.12).
*Uccāvacavācaḥ* means "speaking various kinds of words"; Amarasimha states: *uccāvacaṃ naikabhedam* ("*uccāvaca* means manifold variety").

The word *uccāvacākiñcana* is correct by virtue of its being a *nipātana* (an irregular formation). The word *evam* refers back to the aforementioned hostility (*prātikūlya*). Regarding *saha* and so forth: *nirgatvarībhiḥ* means "having the nature of going out" (*nirgamanaśīlābhiḥ*).

The word *gatvara* is correct by virtue of its being a nipātana (irregular formation); *raudrīm* means fierce (*ugrām*), according to Amara’s lexicon: "the word *raudra* means fierce" (*raudraṃ tūgram*).
[It refers to] the worship on the field of battle.
The sense is "I shall do"; the present tense (*laṭ*) is used here to indicate immediate futurity (*sāmīpye*). From this point onward, [the word] *roṣaṇaḥ*...
The passage ending with "O son of Renuka" (214) is the dramatic element named *toṭaka*, because it consists of extremely angry speech; as it has been said: "An angry utterance is *toṭaka*" (215).
Thus [ends section] 50.
Vāgrūpā is a terrifying figure made of straw and other materials for the purpose of protecting crops; she is constructed from posts and the like,
holding a bow and other weapons, and is intended to frighten away wild animals and the like.
The meaning is that the image of a man [drawn by you] is terrifying to those whose minds are not steadfast in your words.
From this point until the end of the verse with "I have no satisfaction" (217).

Because it consists in the manifestation of one's own power (*svaśakti*), the *oja* is a subsidiary element (*sandhyantara*) of the *sandhi*; as it has been said: "The *oja*, moreover, is the presentation of speech that manifests one's own power" (218). It "transgresses"; namely, the boundary (*maryādā*).

The remainder [of the commentary] follows: *durmanāyante* means they become angry. Unable to endure the excellence indicated by the phrase "the disciple of Rudra" (219), he says "by them," and so forth. The word *śambhoḥ* connects with what precedes.

The sense is this: since my satisfaction does not come from the mere stringing of your preceptor’s bow, but rather from fighting with him, therefore—even though he is not present—you must fight with that very person by means of you yourself, who are the casket containing the entire treasury of his bowcraft; thus, it is a battle with him alone through me. [This refers to] my valor.
Your teacher alone is the object [of devotion], not you; thus, by disregarding your own teacher, one disregards the Teacher himself. //51//
*Saṃrambhaḥ* means anger. The repeated recitation is due to an excess of anger rooted in boastful talk.
"Aho" and so forth; "sarvataḥ" and so forth. While the upward flaming is characteristic of ordinary fire, this one—(220)—is different.
The meaning is that the fire of his wrath blazes on all sides; for this very reason, there is a sense of dreadfulness.
This section begins here and ends with the verse: "Again the sage Bhārgava was enraged" (221).

What is called "anger" (*krodha*) is a subsidiary element (*upāṅga*) known as *sandhyantara*; as it has been said: "Anger, however, is the inflaming of the mind resulting from the perception of an offense or the like. (222) "Be mindful" means "be attentive," which is to say, "prepare yourselves for my battle. [This refers to] me, who have destroyed the Kṣatriyas because of the offense committed by a single Kārtavīrya.
The sense is that the slaughter of all Kṣatriyas was ordained due to the offense committed by two members of the Kṣatriya lineage.
He states this very point with the words beginning "by whom," etc. *Madhvāsava* is a specific type of liquor.
The phrase "even one's mother" expresses a lack of restraint and cruelty;
one who is ignorant of its sweetness does not feel affection for it.
The meaning is that he abandons [them].

The mention of "bones and fragments" is made because of the great wounds. By the word "again," he indicates that his anger was previously withdrawn; by the word "sage" (muni), he indicates that his anger is now unassailable. //52//
Rāma’s laughter [expresses]: "You think, 'I shall frighten him by slandering the king behind his back,' but I am not afraid of that much.
For this very reason, when the fruit of the act of contempt—the act of frightening—resides in the agent, [the rule] "apād... [applies].

The suffix *ātmanepada* is used in the form "apavadase" (you disparage), as in the verse beginning with "nṛpān" (kings). And the invisibility [of those kings] is due to their residing in other continents.
"Apavadase" means you treat with contempt.
The phrase "again enraged" (225), which indicates the act of killing, is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
The expression "child's play" is a statement of his own capability intended to provoke Bhārgava.
*kalā* means skill;
*niḥsṛṣṭārthaḥ* means the purpose of the action; tell me, which arm is it? That...
The construction is: "let him strike. //53//
"Never heard before, never seen before"—this is according to the rule *bhūtapūrve caraṭ* (Pāṇini 5.3.53).
The sense is: "Due to a lapse of time, I have suffered humiliation.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Do you know," etc.: anticipating a specific detail with the word "as," he completes it with "by my father," and so forth. *Arjunī* means a cow.
"māheyī, saurabheyī, gauḥ, usrā, mātā, śṛṅgiṇī, arjunī, aghnyā, and rohiṇī are synonyms for a cow," according to Amara. By that very [definition], he provides the reason for the general application.
Intending specifically the status of a Kṣatriya, he says:
*autsargikaḥ* means "derived from the general rule" (*utsarga*), that is, from the universal (*sāmānya*); [the suffix -ika is applied] according to the rule "derived from that" (Pāṇini 4.3.74).

Thus [ends the discussion of] the suffix *ṭhak*. "Kṣatriyahood" (*kṣatriyatva*) is the subordinate member (*upasarjana*), meaning it is not the primary factor. "Possessing a cause" (*hetumān*) means possessing a motivator. By setting aside the anger that would otherwise arise due to the general rule pertaining to kṣatriyahood—which is the cause for your death—one acts by means of what has been obtained as an exception (*apavāda*).
The meaning is that I was impelled by the very anger born from the breaking of the preceptor’s bow;
for even compared to one's father,
the teacher of knowledge is superior, and thus [my action] was rooted precisely in that anger caused by his insult.
The meaning is that [the latter] is superior.
On this point, Āpastamba says: "For he (the father) begets him through knowledge; that is the superior birth."
"The body alone do the mother and father produce. (229) Here, "he" refers to the teacher of knowledge. //54//
Fame itself is a banner made of cloth; for this very reason, there is the expression "become a tattered rag" (*paṭaccarībhūta*), as in the phrase "a *paṭaccara* is a worn-out garment. (230)
Thus says Amara; "it should be seen," with "valor" being the understood object.
Regarding "that," etc.: *prathana* means battle. //55//

"You will attack" means you come toward us for the purpose of battle and seek combat. The sense is that now I am the aggressor (*yāyin*) and you are the defender (*sthāyin*); however, in the case of a withdrawal (*ākarṣaṇa*), the stakes are exactly the reverse. [The opponent is] powerful.
For he becomes one who goes (hi-yāyin); [the word] *hotṛ* refers to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) and also to "one who consumes" (*bhakṣayitṛ*).
The verbal root is *hu*, meaning "to give" and "to eat" (Dhātupāṭha 2.31).
"Utkhātinī" means uneven; "vimardakṣamā" means fit for battle—that is, level.
By the words "kṣātreṇa" and "brāhmeṇa," Janaka and Viśvāmitra are respectively indicated.

"Let it be," and so forth. *Śaraṇadaḥ* means "the giver of protection"; by metaphorical extension (*lakṣaṇayā*), it signifies being intent on protecting. Amara states: "The word *śaraṇa* [denotes] both a house and a protector.
*Sarvābhisāraḥ* means "the complete mobilization" or "the full array of forces."
According to Amarasimha: "Sarvābhisāraḥ, sarvaughaḥ, and sarvasannahanārthakaḥ" [refer to a general mobilization]. "Vaijayikyaḥ" means those having victory as their purpose.
"Let them provide counter-measures," that is, let them ward it off; the word "defeat" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sense].
The meaning is: "let them be employed for the purpose of preventing the misfortune caused by me. //56//
"Of those spreading forth," meaning "of those employing [it].
"A maiden," and so forth. "In this case as well":
I became the stake for the previous stringing of the bow; what [stake] is there for this one?
By causing Sītā to be agitated with the thought, "Or perhaps another bride-price [is required]," the sight of the sky is the *anubhāva* (consequent effect) of that deliberation.
From the cessation of movement— that is, from the obstruction of the path to the world she must reach— it is understood that Rāma’s arrow is unfailing (*amogha*).
Established convention. //57//

"By others," and so forth. "Of those summoned"—the word "for battle" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. "Enjoined"; the sense is that there is a transgression (pratyavāya) in failing to perform it. "Untrained in weapons" means those who have not practiced with weapons.
By *aṇḍīreṇa* = by a child, meaning by one who is incapable; the *Viśva* lexicon states: "The word *aṇḍīraḥ* [is used] for an incapable man" (234);

and "from *kāṇḍa* and *aṇḍa*, the suffixes *īran* and *īrac* [are applied]" (235). The reference to Rāma in the third person (*rāmeṇa*) is for the purpose of censure. *Guṇitam* = repeated. For children indeed...
"Those who are ignorant of the Dharma. (236) Regarding "asceticism and knowledge":
the intended meaning is that it is only fitting for you, who know the duties of Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, to exercise forbearance in this matter.

From "Starting from here" up to "The joy of victory over Jamadagnya alone is the most auspicious occasion," this is the dramatic element named *saṅgraha* (conciliation), because it consists of the expression of conciliation and bribery (*sāma-dāna*). As it has been said: "Conciliation..."
"The expression of conciliation and bribery" (238). //58//
"Laughter," because of the attribution of guilt to oneself even when one is innocent.
"For which purpose," and so forth; the word "which" (yat) refers back to the examination of the Vaiṣṇava splendor. "Provoked," it is said.
As it is said: "The knowledge of the internal states of those who are asleep, intoxicated, or angry occurs [through yoga].
(239) *Āmaya* is of the nature of reflection for the purpose of removing the burden of the earth; *laghimāna*, [the power of lightness].
This [joy] arises from the absence of that [sorrow], and this is because you have laid down the burden [of the world].
"Something" means that it will be "perfectly so" after the slaying of Rāvaṇa; such is the sense. //59//
"Jāmadagnya. Raising the chin is an expressive gesture (*anubhāva*) of conciliation.
*Āraṇyakas* means those who dwell in the forest (*araṇya*).

"Human beings"; [the suffix] *vuñ* is applied according to the rule "from *araṇya*, [to denote] human beings" (Pāṇini 4.2.129). "Where will you take me?"—previously, for the sake of business, even that which was improper, namely going to the city, had been done; from here...
The sense is that this is not appropriate.

A *vaikhānasa* is a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) who follows the path proclaimed by the sage Vikhanas; his conduct is described as: "living in the forest, subsisting on roots and fruits, and devoted to austerity" (241).
Such is its form.

This has been stated by Gautama: "The Vaikhānasa dwells in the forest, subsisting on roots and fruits, devoted to austerity; having established the Śrāvaṇaka fire, he eats food that is not from the village."
He should worship the gods, humans, and ancestors;
he should be hospitable to all guests; he may subsist on alms, avoiding what is forbidden; he should not stand upon ground ploughed by the plow, nor [enter] a village.
"He should enter [the hermitage]; wearing matted hair and clothed in bark or skins, he should not eat for more than a year. (242) Thus it is said.
Haradatta states: "The *Śrāvaṇaka* is the *Vaikhānasa-sūtra*; according to the method prescribed therein, the single sacred fire (*ekāgni*) is to be established. (243)
The forest-dwelling stage for Bhārgava, who does not marry: "Now, the forest-dweller, being already a celibate student, goes forth [into the life of renunciation]. (244)

This is not contradictory, as the statement from Āpastamba—"the first alternative is that one becomes a forest-dweller directly from the stage of studentship"—indicates this understanding. "Lapse of conduct" refers to such things as entering a village; "conduct" refers to acts such as offering salutations.
"Of whom," and so forth. The "fourfold group" (*caturvarga*) consists of virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), pleasure (*kāma*), and liberation (*mokṣa*).

"Smṛti" refers to a treatise on the instruction of dharma rooted in the Purāṇas; as it is said: "That lord of yogis, residing in Mithilā, having meditated for a moment, spoke to the sages. (245) //60//
"Gāyatrī," and so forth. That *ṛc* which has three quarters (*pāda*)—that is, one-fourth parts of a verse—is "three-footed" (*tripadā*).
The feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied after the word *pāda* by the rule "ṭābṛci" (Pāṇini 4.1.9), as in "pādaḥ."
The word *pat* (247) undergoes the change to *pad*. The *gāyatrī* is well known. The *pāvamānyas* begin with "svādhiṣṭhayā" (248). *Brahman* is austerity (*tapas*).
According to Amarasimha, "The Vedas, reality, austerity, and Brahman" [are synonyms]. May he prosper—that is, may he increase. //61//
*Apattrapā* (modesty) arises from a lapse in conduct.

Regarding the phrase "May they be auspicious" (*śivāḥ santu*), the word "may they be" (*bhavantu*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. By the expression "from their own homes," [the author] dispels the notion that they do not belong to him. [The term] "consisting of virtues" (*guṇamayī*)...
The fulfillment of the state of being a garland [is found] in the sixth [chapter], in the enumeration of the Matsya, Kūrma, and other [Purāṇas]. //62//
The mutual embrace of the two kings [occurs] out of joy at Rāma’s victory. "Sucarita," and so forth. "Aitihāsikas" means those who study history (itihāsa);
the suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule "ākhyānākhyāyikā" (Pāṇini 4.3.87). It will not cease.

The meaning is that they will always provide explanations. Regarding the phrase "from the belly": the implication is that had Bhārgava not been defeated by Rāma, he would have surely destroyed the Kṣatriyas as before.
*Vijitvara* means "having the nature of victory"; [the suffix] *kvarap* is applied according to the rule *iṇ-naś-jis-artibhyaḥ kvarap* (Pāṇini 3.2.163).
The meaning is "the fiery energy of a kṣatriya. //63//
"From long ago," and so forth.
"To be lived upon" (*upajīvyam*) means to be enjoyed. "Superior" (*upari*) means excellent, because he, being of that lineage, has conquered Bhārgava.
The touchstone (*nikaṣa*) is a stone for determining color; for this very reason, it possesses the quality of determining color and the state of being a great hero (*mahāvīratva*). //64//
The office of dharma is the kingdom.

"Capable of bearing all burdens" (*sarvadhurīṇa*) means one who is able to carry every load; the suffix *kha* is applied according to the rule "the suffix *kha* comes after *sarvadhura*" (Pāṇini 4.4.78). By the appropriate method, that is, by the conduct of a sage (*munivṛtti*).
Because it has been stated, "in old age, for those who follow the conduct of sages" (253), [the word] "somewhere" (*kvāpi*) indicates his state of detachment.
"Such as this" refers to one who knows what ought to be done. "In due order" means immediately after the entry into Ayodhyā; this is the intended sense.
"What is the cause? indicates the meaning of the letter;
from here until "she torments her mother" (254), [the section] concerning what is yet to come...

Because it indicates the delay of the consecration as the cause for Rāmacandra’s departure, this is the *śliṣṭa* (double-entendre) *patākāsthānaka*. As it has been said: "Speech that is highly suggestive (*sātiśaya*), double-entendred (*śliṣṭa*), and resting upon the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of poetic composition—this is the second *patākāsthānaka*."
Thus it was proclaimed.
(255) Mantharā is the maidservant of Kaikeyī. The deliberation concerns the subject matter of the reason for sending the letter.
The distress of exile, born of exile, and the fruit of exile—these flash [in his mind]. "Ambā" refers to Kausalyā; "and Sumitrā" also flashes [in his mind].
Regarding the words "that" and so forth: the meaning is that it was already previously accepted—that is, already promised—and is not something new.
"From *ūry-aṅga*, *ūry-uru*, and *arī* [the suffix *ṇamul* is applied], as in *karoti* and *kurute*";
thus it is stated in the *Kriyāratnakośa*. And there is the usage of Śrī Harṣa:
"Indeed, the fist was not one whose binding had been accepted (*urīkṛta-bandhanaḥ*). Regarding the word *varṣāṇi*: [it is used] in the sense of continuous connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*).
The second [stanza]:

(258) The establishment of the location in Daṇḍakā—“Janasthāna is in a certain part of Daṇḍakā, and it is presided over by Khara and others; therefore, in the calamity rooted in the conflict there...”
"With the expectation of [finding] companions, there may be an opportunity to show favor toward Sugrīva"—this was his intention. //65//
Placing a letter upon the head indicates an absence of despondency during a journey (259).
[The passage beginning with] "O child," etc., concerns the matter of propitiation.
"Sahādhyāyinīm" means one who studied together; the sense is "one who was devoted to me just as you are. "Prajāvatī" means the wife of a brother. Regarding "purastāt":
it refers to the first departure of Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa; "that [is what] mine... [so it continues].
Because of the mention of the "two boons" (*varadvayam*) at the beginning of the verse instructing Kaikeyī, and because of the inability to endure delay at the time of departure,
[the word] *samāśvasitam* is used; it is the second person dual middle voice form of the root *śvas*.
"Hand," and so forth. The action consists of the separation of father and son.
"This is such-and-such" means it is of that kind; it is similar to the expression "it is such-and-such."
"Atikrūra" means exceedingly cruel. "Ā" signifies suffering;
as Amarasimha states: "The word 'ā' may be used in the senses of anger and affliction. This [act] is censured by the world.
The sense is: from where has this come about? //66//
"Someone," and so forth. The form *vāṅmanasayoḥ* is a *nipāta* (irregular formation) according to the sūtra *acatur-ādi* (Pāṇini 5.4.77).
*Ativṛttavartmā* means "one who has transcended the path"; [it is] "beyond the scope."
Up to: it is an entity called sorrow;
it is both burning and deluding; therefore, it is something whose specific nature is not determined here.
In this matter, I possess only the status of a consumer, and not the power to provide a remedy;
for the promise that has been made must not be transgressed.
And because you cannot bear separation from me— me, who am thus fallen into doubt due to burning and delusion— it is not right for you to abandon me;
by some means or other, you yourself must turn back from your journey and remedy this.
Existence. //67//
"Having reflected" means [on] the impending misfortune for Rāma together with Sītā during their stay in Daṇḍaka—this is the ellipsis. "Ātitheyī" means hospitable toward guests;
the suffix *ḍhañ* is applied according to the rule "pathyatithi" (Pāṇini 4.4.104).
The suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15); however, the technical maxim (*paribhāṣā*) "when there is a mention of a [suffix] without an *anubandha*,
[it does not include] that with an *anubandha*" does not apply here,
because there is no other suffix without an *anubandha* that serves as the cause for the production of *ṅīp* except for *ḍhañ*.
Because of the absence of the word "ten" (daśa), the result of our entering this house has become merely the service of a Rākṣasa, and not that of sages such as ourselves.
This is an expression of despondency. By this, the giving of alms to Rāvaṇa, who was disguised as a mendicant, is indicated. It is merely a continuation [of their relationship], not a separation;
[it refers to] the suffering of a daughter separated from her husband.
The sense is that it would be unbearable for the parents.

Regarding the passage beginning with "dhanuṣmantau" (the two armed with bows): here, by the first half-verse, he expresses the apprehension of misfortune for Rāma. As for "dhanuṣmantau," one who is indeed equipped with weapons—

They are destroyed. Those regions are the Daṇḍakas, most intensely hot (*ūṣmalatama*), meaning possessed of great heat (*mahoṣmavant*); [the suffix] *lac* is applied after *sidhma* and other words in the sense of possession (Pāṇini 5.2.97).
"Difficult to traverse because of Rāvaṇa’s movements" means that it is hard to pass through.
"A child" refers to one who is ignorant of illusion (*māyā*). "Those of inauspicious conduct" are those full of illusion. "By dear ones" means by those who are exceedingly dear;
sons and others are dear because they are regarded as extensions of the self, whereas the self itself—

The phrase "by being everything that remains" indicates extreme endearment; and because such a sacrifice of life precludes the infamy of abandoning one's son, it reveals the fundamental absence of selfish desire.
"Bhāvaḥ" (the meaning): "Friend"—this is a sarcastic remark; the intended sense is that you have become a stain upon the family. //68//
The comparison to the *tamāla* leaf is due to the well-known blackness of ill-repute. "How shall we see [her]? refers to Janaka’s embarrassment because of his kinship with Kaikeyī.
"Self-composed" (*svastha*) means established in one's natural state, as I hear it to be. Thus...
The word "do" is to be understood as the ellipsis; furthermore, the phrase "residing in heaven" also flashes forth [in the mind].
"Protect me"—the meaning is: by bearing the burden of protecting the subjects, which rests upon me.
"In my lap" (*aṅke*)—because [Rāma's] life-story is directly perceived [by her], even though he has been separated from her during his forest exile.
By the phrase "protect me" (269), which indicates a second consecration, there is a reference back to the previously mentioned consecration of Rāma.
This is because of the connection [established] by this [passage],
and because it serves as the locus for the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of various arrangements, such as the entry of Bhārgava and the giving of the slow-moving letter.
Thus ends the fourth act in the *Anargharāghavapañcikā* composed by Viṣṇu, the son of the venerable Muktinātha.
